Beta diversity of microbes during inulin treatment

Roger Calvas

2025-04-23

Goals

  1. Load in phyloseq data with rooted tree & colors and functions.
  2. Evaluate sequencing depth and remove samples, if needed.
  3. Normalize the read counts between samples.
  4. Calculate community dissimilarities. Numbers between 0 and 1. If 0, completely similar versus if they are 1, then they’re completely dissimilar.
    1. Sorensen: Shared Species as a binary value: Abundance-unweighted
    2. Bray-Curtis: Shared Abundant species: Abundance-weighted
    3. (Abundance-)Weighted UNIFRAC: Consider Abundant Species and where they fall on the tree
  5. Run statistics with functions from the vegan R package:
    1. PERMANOVA with adonis2().
    2. betadispR with betadisper() and permutest().
  6. Visualize the community data with two unconstrained Ordinations:
    1. PCoA: Linear Method. Eigenvalue = how much variation is explained by each axis. Choose to view axis 1, 2, 3, etc. and plot them together.
    2. NMDS: Non-linear. Smush multiple Dimensions into 2 or 3 axes. Need to report Stress value (ideally <0.15).

Inputs

  1. We will need the phytree_preprocessed_physeq.RData

Outputs

This is an exciting analysis!!! We get to answer another one of our scientific questions!

  1. Calculated beta-diversity dissimilarity measures (e.g. Sorensen, Bray-Curtis, abundance-unweighted and -weighted UniFrac) across every sample.
  2. Ordination figures (i.e., PCoA/NMDS) to include in the scientific paper that visualize the data as it relates to the scientific question.
  3. Statistical tests (i.e., PERMANOVA & betadisper) conveying the measured and quantified changes and patterns in biodiversity.

Scientific Question

Does inulin treatment increase SCFA production (i.e., acetate, butyrate, propionate), and is this associated with a shift in fiber-fermenting bacteria?

  • Null Hypothesis: Microbial diversity and scfa production does not vary during inulin treatment.
  • Alternative Hypothesis: An inulin treatment will stimulate scfa production and shift microbial composition.

INTERPRETATION #1: What is your scientific question and hypotheses? Do they relate to abundance? Presence/absence? Phylogeny?

Does inulin treatment increase SCFA production (i.e., acetate, butyrate, propionate), and is this associated with a shift in fiber-fermenting bacteria?

  • Null Hypothesis: Microbial diversity and scfa production does not vary during inulin treatment.
  • Alternative Hypothesis: An inulin treatment will stimulate scfa production and shift microbial composition.

This question relates to abundance by observing changes in the gut microbial composition during an inulin treatment, favoring the taxa that produce scfa from fermentable fiber. # Set up

# What time did we start running this script? 
start_time <- Sys.time()

Set the seed

set.seed(39809473)

Load Packages, colors & functions

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, devtools, phyloseq, patchwork, vegan, 
               install = FALSE)

# Load Colors 
source("code/colors.R")

# Load functions 
source("code/functions.R")

1. Load in the data

# load phyloseq object
load("data/04_Phylogenetic_Tree/archaeal_rooted_physeq.RData")
archaeal_rooted_physeq
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 1980 taxa and 161 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 161 samples by 54 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 1980 taxa by 9 taxonomic ranks ]
## phy_tree()    Phylogenetic Tree: [ 1980 tips and 1979 internal nodes ]
# Intuition check on seq depth
min(sample_sums(archaeal_rooted_physeq))
## [1] 7215

Create metadata

# Create Metadata_df 
metadata_df <- 
  archaeal_rooted_physeq %>%
  sample_data() %>%
  data.frame()

Normalizing the Read Depth

2. Explore the Raw Read Counts

# calculate read counts per sample 
raw_TotalSeqs_df <- 
  archaeal_rooted_physeq %>%
  # Calculate the total number of sequences/reads
  sample_sums() %>%
  data.frame()

# Take a look 
head(raw_TotalSeqs_df)
##                .
## SRR6443836 19399
## SRR6443839 27322
## SRR6443844  9565
## SRR6443871 28582
## SRR6443905 15277
## SRR6443910 16349
# Rename the column 
colnames(raw_TotalSeqs_df)[1] <- "TotalSeqs"

# add a new column of num_ASVs (RAW, non-noramlized # ASVs)
raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df <- 
  raw_TotalSeqs_df %>%
  mutate(num_ASVs = colSums(otu_table(archaeal_rooted_physeq) > 1))

#View(raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df)

# Plot histogram of seq depth 
rawSeq_histogram <- 
  raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TotalSeqs)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 35000)) + 
  labs(title = "Raw Seq Depth Histogram") + 
  theme_bw()

# Plot Seq Depth versus num_ASVs
rawSeq_vs_numASV_plot <- 
  raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = num_ASVs, y = TotalSeqs)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 35000)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  labs(title = "Seq Depth vs # ASVs") + 
  theme_bw()

# is it significant? 
summary(lm(TotalSeqs ~ num_ASVs, data = raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df))
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = TotalSeqs ~ num_ASVs, data = raw_TotalSeqsASVs_df)
## 
## Residuals:

## ---

## 
## Residual standard error: 5209 on 159 degrees of freedom

## F-statistic: 26.92 on 1 and 159 DF,  p-value: 6.373e-07
# Put the two plots together.
rawSeq_histogram + rawSeq_vs_numASV_plot +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

INTERPRETATION #2: Evaluating the above plots, what did you scale the read counts to in your dataset? Why did you choose that number? Do you think it is sufficient to perform a beta-diversity analysis and accurately compare your data to one another?

I chose the minimun sequencing depth in the dataset at 7k~ because even thought plot B shows a positive correlation between sequencing depth and number of ASVs but it is not too steep, also based on the spread of the scatterplot and the fact that the minimum is not an outlier it seems like sufficient lenght. There is an outlier with unusually high count of ASVs so I will keep an eye on it.

INTERPRETATION #3: Evaluate the scaled read count plots above. Are the total number of sequences across all of your samples in the same general range? What is the minimum and maximum (i.e., the range) of the sequencing depth? How was the relationship with the number of ASVs modified after scaling the read counts?

They are all in the same range, the minimum is 7191 and the maximum is 7229 ( range of 38), the range is 0.5~% which is really good. The relationship stayed quite similar after scaling, with the scatter plot distribution skewing a bit to the left including the outlier sample with the most ASVs. ## sorting out NA values Since almost a 3rd of the propionate values are missing and this unables me to do a permanova with total_scfa I will do a simple imputation to change the NA values of all the scfas and calculate the total_scfa again with the sum

## sorting out NA values
# Impute missing values in acetate with median
metadata_df$acetate[is.na(metadata_df$acetate)] <- median(metadata_df$acetate, na.rm = TRUE)

# Impute missing values in butyrate with median
metadata_df$Butyrate[is.na(metadata_df$Butyrate)] <- median(metadata_df$Butyrate, na.rm = TRUE)

#Impute missing values in propionate with the median 
metadata_df$propionate[is.na(metadata_df$propionate)] <- median(metadata_df$propionate, na.rm = TRUE)

# Recalculate total SCFA
metadata_df$total_scfa <- metadata_df$acetate + metadata_df$Butyrate + metadata_df$propionate

#Intuition check
sum(is.na(metadata_df$acetate))      
## [1] 0
sum(is.na(metadata_df$Butyrate))  
## [1] 0
sum(is.na(metadata_df$propionate))
## [1] 0
sum(is.na(metadata_df$total_scfa))   
## [1] 0

INTERPRETATION #4: Which dissimilarity metric is most related to your scientific question? Why or why not?

I think bray curtis would be the most related to my scientific question, since I am looking for shifts in the dinamics of the community I want to look closely into relative abundance changes during the treatment, also find specific taxa that increased in response to inulin and that are related to scfa production from fermentable fiber, unifrac is a close second because I want to see the shifts in the structure of the community.

Permanova continous variable with total_scfa

# bray
## 1. Run with by = terms for R² values, sensitive to order of variables! 
## ALWAYS check and confirm the order of your terms and how they interact with each other.  
bray_status_adonis_terms1 <- adonis2(scaled_Bray_dist ~ status + total_scfa, data = metadata_df, by = "terms")
bray_status_adonis_terms1
## Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## adonis2(formula = scaled_Bray_dist ~ status + total_scfa, data = metadata_df, by = "terms")
##             Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)
## status       1    0.356 0.00834 1.3391  0.159
## total_scfa   1    0.326 0.00764 1.2274  0.217
## Residual   158   41.980 0.98402              
## Total      160   42.662 1.00000
# Check the order of the terms
bray_status_adonis_terms2 <- adonis2(scaled_Bray_dist ~ total_scfa + status, data = metadata_df, by = "terms")
bray_status_adonis_terms2

INTERPRETATION #5: Using the above example to guide you, run the appropriate PERMANOVA for your scientific question and interpret the results. What biological conclusion can you draw from your PERMANOVA results?

Across all models status explained 0.8% of the variation, so the inulin treatment may not be statistically significant but it may change the microbial composition in specific reproducible ways, aditionally all results had a high R^2 values meaning that the results may be explained by specific abundance changes in certain taxa. While status itself only explains a small portion of the variation scfa_production seems to be linked to the community shifts so it may be related to functional potential.

5b. Betadisper: Testing Variances/Dispersions

Sorensen

# Homogeneity of Disperson test with beta dispr
# Sorensen Betadisper - status 
dispr_sorensen_status <- betadisper(scaled_sorensen_dist, metadata_df$status)
# permutest() performs a non-parametric permutation test, which is robust and valid for the kind of data used in beta diversity analysis (e.g., dissimilarity matrices).
permutest(dispr_sorensen_status)
## 
## Permutation test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersions
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## Response: Distances
##            Df  Sum Sq   Mean Sq      F N.Perm Pr(>F)
## Groups      1 0.00114 0.0011413 0.2072    999  0.647
## Residuals 159 0.87580 0.0055082
# Sorensen Betadisper - propionate
dispr_sorensen_propionate<- betadisper(scaled_sorensen_dist, metadata_df$propionate)
permutest(dispr_sorensen_propionate)

## Residuals 159 1.6538 0.0104013
# Bray-Curtis Betadisper - propionate 
dispr_bray_propionate <- betadisper(scaled_Bray_dist, metadata_df$propionate)
permutest(dispr_bray_propionate)
## 
## Permutation test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersions
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## Response: Distances
##            Df Sum Sq  Mean Sq      F N.Perm Pr(>F)   
## Groups    112 8.6176 0.076943 5.7385    999  0.002 **
## Residuals  48 0.6436 0.013408                        
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
# Bray-Curtis Betadisper - Butyrate  
dispr_bray_Butyrate <- betadisper(scaled_Bray_dist, metadata_df$Butyrate)
permutest(dispr_bray_Butyrate)
## 
## Permutation test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersions
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## Response: Distances
##            Df  Sum Sq   Mean Sq      F N.Perm Pr(>F)
## Groups    154 1.48459 0.0096402 3.3983    999  0.758
## Residuals   6 0.01702 0.0028368

INTERPRETATION #6: Using the above example to guide you, run the appropriate betadisper() and permutest() for your scientific question and interpret the results. What biological conclusion can you draw from your dispersion analysis?

Based on the dispersion analysis I can conclude that only propionate has significant dispersion making propionate analysis less rigid, while all the other variables had not significant dispersion so their anova is valid.

INTERPRETATION #7: Taking into account both the betadisper()/permutest() and the PERMANOVA (adonis2()) test that you ran, what biological conclusion can you draw regarding your data?

Given all the test results I can conclude that inulin has a small not-statistical significant effect on scfa concentrations, aditioanlly it has a relevant effect on microbial composition that can further explored.even if the permanova was not significant the difference is not explained by dispersion and it could account for true biological difference.

PCoA: Principal Coordinate analysis

### SORENSEN 
# First, calculate PCoA with Soresen
scaled_soren_pcoa <- 
  ordinate(physeq = scaled_physeq,
         method = "PCoA",
         distance = "bray", binary = TRUE)

# Take a quick look
str(scaled_soren_pcoa)
## List of 5
##  $ correction: chr [1:2] "none" "1"
##  $ note      : chr "No correction was applied to the negative eigenvalues"
##  $ values    :'data.frame':  161 obs. of  6 variables:
##   ..$ Eigenvalues   : num [1:161] 4.7 2.43 1.98 1.78 1.7 ...
##   ..$ Relative_eig  : num [1:161] 0.1475 0.0762 0.062 0.0558 0.0533 ...
##   ..$ Rel_corr_eig  : num [1:161] 0.1099 0.0576 0.0472 0.0426 0.0407 ...
##   ..$ Broken_stick  : num [1:161] 0.0355 0.0292 0.0261 0.024 0.0224 ...
##   ..$ Cum_corr_eig  : num [1:161] 0.11 0.167 0.215 0.257 0.298 ...
##   ..$ Cumul_br_stick: num [1:161] 0.0355 0.0648 0.0909 0.1149 0.1373 ...
##  $ vectors   : num [1:161, 1:100] -0.0955 -0.2796 -0.1706 -0.1674 -0.2247 ...
##   ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
##   .. ..$ : chr [1:161] "SRR6443836" "SRR6443839" "SRR6443844" "SRR6443871" ...
##   .. ..$ : chr [1:100] "Axis.1" "Axis.2" "Axis.3" "Axis.4" ...
##  $ trace     : num 31.9
##  - attr(*, "class")= chr "pcoa"
#prework for triplot ( I am going to go back and re do a couple of steps considering that I am pruning the 51 NA samples instead of imputing, alpha diversity as well, for now I will finish the hw :())
###  Subset to samples with non-missing total_scfa
# Filter the scaled object to remove samples with NA total_scfa
physeq_no_na <- subset_samples(scaled_physeq, !is.na(total_scfa))
## subsetted distance object
subset_soren_dist <- distance(physeq_no_na, method = "bray", binary = TRUE)
## PCoA with vegan object
vegan_pcoa_soren <- capscale(subset_soren_dist ~ 1)
## Fit vector 
scfa_vector_fit_soren <- envfit(vegan_pcoa_soren, sample_data(physeq_no_na)$total_scfa, permutations = 999)
scfa_arrow_soren <- as.data.frame(scores(scfa_vector_fit_soren, display = "vectors"))
scfa_arrow_soren$variable <- "total_scfa"
# Rename to match the axis names in ordination_df_soren
colnames(scfa_arrow_soren)[1:2] <- c("CAP1", "CAP2")

## Prepare for plotting the vector 
ordination_df_soren <- as.data.frame(scores(vegan_pcoa_soren, display = "sites"))
colnames(ordination_df_soren)[1:2] <- c("CAP1", "CAP2")
ordination_df_soren$total_scfa <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$total_scfa
ordination_df_soren$status <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$status
ordination_df_soren$host_subject_id <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$host_subject_id

# Variation explained per axis
## Extract eigenvalues from capscale ordination
eig_vals_soren <- vegan_pcoa_soren$CA$eig

## Calculate % variance explained by CAP1 and CAP2
var_exp_soren <- round(100 * eig_vals_soren / sum(eig_vals_soren), 1)

## Create axis labels
xlab_text_soren <- paste0("Axis 1 (", var_exp_soren[1], "%)")
ylab_text_soren <- paste0("Axis 2 (", var_exp_soren[2], "%)")

# Plot it: Sorensen PCoA  
sorensen_pcoa_plot <- 
  ggplot(ordination_df_soren, aes(x = CAP1, y = CAP2)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = host_subject_id), color = "gray80", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(color = total_scfa, shape = status), size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85, stroke = 0.2) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = c("grey80", "darkgreen", "green")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16,17))+
  geom_segment(data = scfa_arrow_soren, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = CAP1, yend = CAP2), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed"), color = "lightgreen", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = scfa_arrow_soren,
            aes(x = CAP1 -0.02, y = CAP2 -0.1, label = variable), color = "lightgreen", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Triplot: soren", x = xlab_text_soren, y = ylab_text_soren, color = "Total SCFA (mmol/kg)", shape = "status") +
  annotate("text",
           x = Inf, y = -Inf,
           label = "SCFA fit: R² = 0.017, p = 0.381",
           hjust = 1.1, vjust = -1.2,
           size = 3.5, fontface = "italic", color = "darkgreen") +
  theme_bw()

### Bray-Curtis 
# Second, calculate PCoA with Bray-Curtis
scaled_bray_pcoa <- 
  ordinate(physeq = scaled_physeq,
         method = "PCoA",
         distance = "bray", binary = FALSE)


## subsetted distance object
subset_bray_dist <- distance(physeq_no_na, method = "bray", binary = FALSE)
## PCoA with vegan object
vegan_pcoa_bray <- capscale(subset_bray_dist ~ 1)
## Fit vector 
scfa_vector_fit_bray <- envfit(vegan_pcoa_bray, sample_data(physeq_no_na)$total_scfa, permutations = 999)
scfa_arrow_bray <- as.data.frame(scores(scfa_vector_fit_bray, display = "vectors"))
scfa_arrow_bray$variable <- "total_scfa"
# Rename to match the axis names in ordination_df_bray
colnames(scfa_arrow_bray)[1:2] <- c("CAP1", "CAP2")

## Prepare for plotting the vector

colnames(ordination_df_bray)[1:2] <- c("CAP1", "CAP2")
ordination_df_bray$total_scfa <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$total_scfa
ordination_df_bray$status <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$status
ordination_df_bray$host_subject_id <- sample_data(physeq_no_na)$host_subject_id

# Variation explained per axis
## Extract eigenvalues from capscale ordination
eig_vals_bray <- vegan_pcoa_bray$CA$eig

## Calculate % variance explained by CAP1 and CAP2
var_exp_bray <- round(100 * eig_vals_bray / sum(eig_vals_bray), 1)

## Create axis labels
xlab_text_bray <- paste0("Axis 1 (", var_exp_bray[1], "%)")
ylab_text_bray <- paste0("Axis 2 (", var_exp_bray[2], "%)")

# Plot it: braysen PCoA  
bray_pcoa_plot <- 
  ggplot(ordination_df_bray, aes(x = CAP1, y = CAP2)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = host_subject_id), color = "gray80", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(color = total_scfa, shape = status), size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85, stroke = 0.2) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = c("grey80", "darkgreen", "green")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16,17))+
  geom_segment(data = scfa_arrow_bray, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = CAP1, yend = CAP2), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed"), color = "lightgreen", linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = scfa_arrow_bray,
            aes(x = CAP1 -0.02, y = CAP2 -0.1, label = variable), color = "lightgreen", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Triplot: bray", x = xlab_text_bray, y = ylab_text_bray, color = "Total SCFA (mmol/kg)", shape = "status") +
  theme_bw() +
    annotate("text",
           x = Inf, y = -Inf,
           label = "SCFA fit: R² = 0.028, p = 0.210",
           hjust = 1.1, vjust = -1.2,
           size = 3.5, fontface = "italic", color = "darkgreen")


print(scfa_vector_fit_soren)

INTERPRETATION #8: Plot your data using a PCoA. Interpret what you can conclude from the PCoA. There is no strong clustering of samples by treatment with bray curtis clustering apparently because of scfa concentrations, and there is minimal correlation between community shifts and total_scfa levels, bray-curtis has a higher percentage explained in each axis and a stronger scfa vector, but still not statistically significant. Neither reveal strong correlations between total SCFA production and community composition. This suggests that the small but consistent changes in each scfa are probably caused within individuals or by changes in functional potential.

INTERPRETATION #10: Plot both the PCoA and NMDS together. Which of the two visualizations work best for your data? Explain your reasoning.

Neither plot shows a strong correlation to the treatment groups, but PCoA has better potential at explaining the differences in the data with some trends and directionality observed. Bray curtis PCoA showed clustering around the top right with a noticeable gradient possibly related to SCFA levels, NMDS showd clustering but most samples were overlapping with no clear trends.
